newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN ECONOMY HAS NO NEED FOR RATE CUT - POLL.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN ECONOMY HAS NO NEED FOR RATE CUT - POLL.

text.p: Steady improvement in the German economy will leave the Bundesbank no reason to provide additional stimulation when it meets to consider monetary policy on Thursday, economists said on Tuesday.

All 10 economists polled by Reuters who closely follow the Bundesbank said they expected the German central bank to keep rates on hold at its regular council meeting this week and indeed for the rest of the year.
"Interest rates are already low," said Stefan Schneider, economist at Banque Paribas in Frankfurt. "The economy is recovering and there is thus no need to cut interest rates."
The German discount rate stands at a historic low 2.5 percent, the emergency Lombard lending rate at 4.5 percent and the securities repurchase rate, or repo, at 3.0 percent.
Economists were also in agreement that the Bundesbank will keep the repo at a fixed rate again on Thursday. The key money market rate was last cut in late August.

The wide-spread consensus on rates comes at a time when Bundesbank council members have sent at times mixed signals about the future of interest rates, some saying they would consider supporting a rate cut if the economy slowed.
But the economists polled by Reuters saw little immediate threat of a slowdown in the economy.
"The economy is recovering quite nicely and is quite happy with interest rates as well," said Robert Prior, economist at James Capel.

Recent economic indicators have shown that German exports, helped by a weaker mark, are starting to pick up. Exports have historically been the first part of the German economy to recover from slower periods, followed by an increase in investment and after that by increases in spending.

Germany's six leading economic research institutes have meanwhile added to the optimism, reporting last week that they see the economy growing 2.5 percent next year after 1.5 percent this year -- solid if unimpressive growth.

The Bundesbank's key policy indicator, M3 money supply, is also giving the central bank scant reason to cut rates, making steady progress toward the top end of Bundesbank's target corridor of between four and seven percent growth.
In September, M3 money supply grew at a 8.4 percent pace, down from 8.7 percent the month before.

"Money supply growth is slowing and is going in the direction of the target corridor," said Nikolaus Keis, economist at Bayerische Vereinsbank. "At the moment there is a harmonious environment for the Bundesbank."
Others said it might be getting harder for the Bundesbank to consider cutting rates when other nations such as the U.K. are lifting theirs.
"Why should rates be reduced when English rates are climbing?" said Wilfried Bock, economist at Norddeutsche Landesbank.
